articles.description:
Two articles back, we covered cookie+nonce authentication, and last time we looked at how WordPress's login cookie is actually a hybrid: signature verification is fully self-contained, but revocation depends on a server-side list of valid tokens. This time we look at the opposite end of the design spectrum: JWT (JSON Web Token), which aims for authentication that is fully stateless — no server-side token list at all. Comparing it against WordPress's hybrid model makes the trade-off between stateful and stateless authentication much easier to see.
A JWT looks like a single string split into three parts by dots — xxxxx.yyyyy.zzzzz. These correspond to a header, a payload, and a signature. The header names the signing algorithm (such as HS256) and token type; the payload holds "claims" — piec…

articles.author: Mohammadreza Alamnejad
articles.description:
Tenant scoping that fails closed, permissions that know about branches, and the tests that keep both honest.
Key takeaways
Resolve the tenant from the session, never from the request. A URL slug or header can select which of your memberships to use, but the server must verify that membership.
Next.js middleware is a gate, not a guard. Use it for redirects and cheap checks; do real authorization next to the data, in your Node API or server code.
Every Server Action and Route Handler is a public endpoint. Authorize inside each one, every time.
Make the database refuse cross-tenant reads. PostgreSQL row-level security with a transaction-local setting means a forgotten filter returns nothing instead of someone else's data.
Permissions are (action, scope), not role names. "Can approve purchases…

articles.author: ThatcherCole8235
articles.description:
A welcome email should leave the request path quickly, but accepting a job is not the same as delivering a message. The reliable design is a small Node.js service wrapper around a direct email API, backed by a durable queue, a suppression check, stored provider message IDs, and polling for delivery events. Do not build this around SMTP when the chosen capability is API-only. The API boundary gives the application enough structure to decide what may be retried and what must be suppressed.
TL;DR: enqueue one idempotent welcome-email job, check suppression immediately before each send, persist the returned message ID, and poll message events into a local delivery record. A bounce should update suppression before another queued job can target that address. This favors correctness over instant …
articles.title: Express.js Transactional Email Service Wrapper: 5 Retry and Logging Layers

articles.description:
My GitHub App takes a pull request, asks an LLM to review it, and posts the comments back. The first time I ran it end to end against a real repository, the review showed up on the PR exactly as intended. Then I opened GitHub's webhook delivery log and found the delivery marked as failed.
Both things were true at once: the feature worked, and the delivery had failed. That contradiction is the interesting part, and the fix I reached for first created a worse problem than the one it solved. This post walks through both, with the code, because the second problem is the kind that doesn't announce itself.
The stack is Next.js (App Router) on Vercel, Drizzle and Postgres, but nothing below depends on those. If you run slow work behind a webhook on a serverless platform, you will meet the same sh…

articles.author: PENG YONG
articles.description:
Why I Built This


A friend told me his face shape was better than mine.
I'm not going to argue with him — I have no data. So I went looking for one of those "what's your face shape" tools. Every single one wanted me to upload a photo of my face. To a server. Run by someone I don't know.
Look, I'm a developer. I know what happens to uploaded images. I've written the code that stores them. I did not want a photo of my own face sitting in someone's bucket with a Date.now() filename and an ACL I can't see.
So I built the version I wanted: one that measures your face and never uploads it. Not "we delete it after 24 hours" — the photo literally never leaves the browser tab. It goes into a canvas, MediaPipe reads it locally, and that's the end of it.
It's called FaceRuler. It's free. There's no …
